title: Thank the freed slave
hook: Epictetus, lame and once enslaved, taught an emperor through a book

segments.voice: Yesterday: a year on the porch, back to the handbook where we started. Your line was a year on the porch. What did your first page say? Day six hundred ninety.

Think about who you'd expect to teach an emperor. A famous senator, maybe. A celebrated scholar with a big house. Now picture the opposite: a boy born in a small city in what's now Turkey, born into slavery, owned by a powerful official in Nero's Rome, walking with a limp. He never writes a book. He's eventually freed, teaches in Rome, gets thrown out of the city with the other philosophers, and starts a school in a provincial town in Greece. Within a generation of his death, the man who will become emperor of Rome is reading his words, and later thanks the friend who lent them to him. Today begins three days of thanks. Today: thank the freed slave.
screen: `BORN INTO SLAVERY, WALKING WITH A LIMP.` → `FREED, EXILED, TEACHING IN GREECE.` → `AN EMPEROR READING HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, his name. Epictetus, in Greek Epiktētos, simply means acquired, the kind of name given to someone who'd been bought. We don't know what his parents called him. He was owned by Epaphroditus, a freedman who served Nero, and at some point was allowed to study with the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus. Second, his limp. Ancient writers didn't agree on how it happened. One later story says a cruel master twisted his leg until it broke, while Epictetus calmly warned him it would. Others say it was illness. Nobody knows for sure. What we know is that the man who taught that lameness hinders the leg, not the will, was speaking from his own body. Third, the book he didn't write. Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian, a young man who later became a governor and historian, took notes on his lectures and published them: the Discourses and the little Handbook we opened this year with. Fourth, the emperor. In the first book of the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher Rusticus for many things, among them for introducing him to Epictetus's discourses, lending them from his own library. So the chain goes: an enslaved boy, a teacher, a student's notes, a friend's loan, an emperor's notebook, and, nearly two thousand years later, you. The most unlikely person in that chain is the one at the start. That's worth a moment of thanks. And it's worth wondering who the unlikely teachers in your own life have been.
screen: `EPIKTĒTOS: ACQUIRED.` · `THE LIMP: SOURCES DIFFER.` · `ARRIAN'S NOTES, NOT HIS BOOK.` · `RUSTICUS LENT MARCUS THE DISCOURSES.` · then, large: `THE UNLIKELY TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something important, but who you never would have expected to. A grandparent with little schooling. A coworker everyone overlooked. A child. A stranger on a bus. Someone you once looked down on. Picture them clearly. What did they teach you, in words or just by how they lived? Let a feeling of thanks rise toward them. If they're still living, think how you might tell them. The bell holds the time.
Thank the freed slave: thanks to Epictetus, born into slavery, lame, who never wrote a book and still taught an emperor, and us. Today's word.
Your line: the unlikely teacher. Thank one unlikely teacher today, in person, by message, or if that's no longer possible, by telling someone about them. Day six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Readers of Epictetus often remember that he was born enslaved and never wrote anything, and some use that as a prompt to thank the unlikely people who have taught them.

fork.setup: you're Arrian, a young student, listening to Epictetus. what do you do that changes history?
options: write down his lectures and publish them
fork.reveal: Arrian's notes became the Discourses and the Handbook; without them, we'd have almost nothing of Epictetus.

original.note: Greek: Epictetus, a name meaning acquired.

trapdoor: what you thought: Epictetus was a famous philosopher who wrote Stoic books.
what it means: he was born enslaved, lame, wrote nothing, and reached an emperor through a student's notes.

what a scholar hears: epiktētos means acquired; he was owned by Nero's freedman Epaphroditus; Origen's Against Celsus 7.53 tells the leg story; Meditations 1.7 thanks Rusticus for the hypomnēmata of Epictetus.

sources.ref: Arrian, letter to Lucius Gellius (preface to the Discourses)

notes: Epictetus's birthplace Hierapolis in Phrygia (modern Turkey), c. 50–55 AD; owner Epaphroditus; studied with Musonius Rufus; expelled from Rome under Domitian (c. 89 or 93–95 AD; Gellius 15.11); school at Nicopolis in Epirus. Confirm details.
Leg story: Celsus via Origen, Against Celsus 7.53; the Suda says rheumatism. Confirm.
Arrian took notes and published them (his prefatory letter to Lucius Gellius); Arrian later a governor (Cappadocia) and historian. Confirm.
Meditations 1.7: Rusticus gave Marcus Epictetus's commentaries from his own collection. Confirm.
Within a generation: Epictetus died c. 135; Marcus likely met his work through Rusticus in the 140s, before becoming emperor in 161. Confirm.
